analysis.one_liner: Restores taxes on polluting industries to fund cleanup of toxic waste sites.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund program cleans up the nation's worst hazardous waste sites. It was originally paid for by taxes on the petroleum and chemical companies whose pollution created those sites, but those taxes lapsed in 1995, leaving taxpayers and the general budget to cover cleanup. This bill would reinstate the petroleum-based hazardous substance excise tax and a corporate environmental income tax through 2016 to refill the cleanup fund.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near hazardous waste sites and taxpayers generally: the industries responsible for toxic contamination would pay to clean it up again, rather than the cost falling on the general federal budget. Communities waiting for Superfund cleanups would have a dedicated funding stream restored.
analysis.who_pays: Petroleum companies, which would again pay the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate on crude oil and petroleum products [S3], and large corporations generally, which would again owe the corporate environmental income tax on their taxable income through 2016 [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Petroleum and chemical companies that would have paid the reinstated taxes were better off; cleanup costs stayed with the general federal budget, paid by taxpayers.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the Superfund excise tax and corporate environmental income tax through 2016 [S1] [S3].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 28, 2005 and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no report to the House [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee never moved the bill [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill reinstated the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate, an excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products that expired in 1995, to refill the toxic site cleanup fund [S3]. Its gain from the bill dying is money that would otherwise have gone to cleaning up hazardous waste.

The bill reinstated the corporate environmental income tax, which had applied to corporate taxable income until it lapsed in 1995, through 2016 [S2] [S3]. With the bill dead, corporations avoided this tax and the cleanup burden remained on the general budget.
